title: SwiftUI view identity and lifetime
summary: SwiftUI must know if a view is "the same one" as before. Same identity = update it and keep its state. New identity = destroy the old one (state lost) and create a new one.
body: **In simple words:** Because views are recreated all the time, SwiftUI uses **identity** to connect a new view value to the old on-screen view and its `@State`.

**Two kinds of identity:** **Structural** - the view's position in the code (first child of this VStack, the `if` branch vs the `else` branch). **Explicit** - an id you give: `ForEach(items, id: \.id)` or `.id(value)`.

**Why it matters:** an `if/else` that shows the same kind of view in both branches actually creates two different views. Switching branches resets state and plays a transition. If you just want to change how it looks, use a modifier with a condition instead.
**Lists:** `ForEach` needs stable, unique ids. Using array indices or `\.self` on duplicate values causes wrong rows to animate, keep wrong state, or flicker.
**`.id(value)`:** changing it forces a brand-new view - handy to reset a form or scroll position, harmful in lists (rebuilds everything).
**`AnyView`** hides the type, so SwiftUI loses structural information and diffs less efficiently. Avoid it in lists.
keyPoints: Identity links view values to on-screen views and their state.
Changing identity resets `@State` and triggers transitions.
Use stable unique ids (model ids, not indices).
Prefer conditional modifiers over `if/else` to keep identity.

code.caption: Keep identity with a modifier

mistakes: Adding `.id(UUID())` - a new identity every render, so state is always lost.
followups: **View lifetime vs state lifetime vs body calls?** `body` can run many times; the view (identity) lives while on screen; `@State` lives as long as the identity.
**Why did my animation not run?** Possibly the identity changed, so SwiftUI inserted a new view instead of animating the old one.
